If you take blood thinners, do not start ibuprofen, naproxen or other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medicines yourself: the combination can increase the risk of bleeding.
Do not combine opioids with sleeping tablets or sedatives without your doctor’s agreement: this can cause dangerous drowsiness and slowed breathing.
Do not drink alcohol or drive while taking strong painkillers.
Keep medicines out of the reach of children and other people; ask your pharmacist what to do with any left over.
If you need painkillers for longer than expected, discuss it with your doctor.
The person is hard to wake, breathing becomes slow or shallow, or there is sudden breathlessness or chest pain — in hospital, call the staff immediately; at home, call an ambulance on 101.
The pain suddenly gets much worse, is not relieved by the prescribed medicines, or other new symptoms appear — see a doctor urgently.

After Surgery: Warning Signs
Sudden breathlessness, chest pain or heavy bleeding: call an ambulance on 101.
After spine surgery, new leg weakness or urinary problems: go to emergency immediately.
Fever of 38 °C or higher, wound redness or discharge: see a doctor today.
Call 101 (Magen David Adom) right away
Three levels of urgency: 101, the emergency department (ER), contact on the same day
sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, or coughing up blood — this may be a blood clot in the lung (CDC);
loss of consciousness, seizures, or sudden severe confusion;
heavy bleeding from the wound that does not stop when you press on it;
a foot or leg that suddenly becomes cold, pale, or blue, especially with severe pain, new numbness, or weakness — this may mean that blood flow is blocked (Society for Vascular Surgery);
after neck surgery: rapidly increasing neck swelling, difficulty breathing, or a sudden inability to swallow saliva (Cambridge University Hospitals).
Go to the emergency department (ER) immediately

After spine surgery, new or rapidly worsening weakness or numbness in an arm or leg, numbness around the genitals, between the legs, or around the anus (saddle area), being unable to urinate, or new loss of bladder or bowel control must be checked immediately in an emergency department (ER). Do not wait for a scheduled visit or for a reply from the ward. If your condition is getting worse quickly, or you cannot get there safely on your own, call an ambulance on 101.
(Source: Guy's and St Thomas' NHS)
Pain that suddenly gets much worse and does not go away with the pain medicine you were prescribed, or your leg is in an unusual position.

If you develop new pain, swelling, redness or warmth in your calf or thigh, especially on one side, go to the emergency department immediately: these may be signs of a blood clot. Call an ambulance on 101 for sudden shortness of breath or chest pain (CDC; NICE NG89; NICE NG158).
Contact the ward or see a doctor the same day

If your temperature reaches 38 °C or higher, stays high or keeps coming back, or you have chills, contact the ward where you had your operation or get medical care the same day. If you are feeling worse overall, get help no matter what the thermometer says (AAOS).

Redness, heat, swelling, or tenderness around the wound that is getting worse, pus or unusual discharge, a dressing that keeps soaking through, a bad smell, or the edges of the wound coming apart all need to be examined the same day (AAOS; NICE NG125).
Moderate pain, and slight swelling and bruising around the wound, are common after surgery and slowly get better. If you are not sure, call the ward.
The wound and preventing blood clots

Do not remove or change the dressing yourself unless the ward told you to. Whether you can shower depends on the type of dressing and the condition of the wound. Follow the instructions you were given at discharge (NICE NG125).

If you were prescribed medicines to prevent blood clots or compression stockings, follow the plan from your discharge papers. Do not stop the medicines on your own. If the stockings cause pain, strong squeezing, blisters, or a change in skin color, stop using them and contact medical staff right away. If you use stockings, check your skin every day (NICE NG89).
Move and walk as you were advised.

A tube by the wound
After surgery you may have a drain: a thin tube that comes out from the operated area and is connected to a container. Not everyone gets one. The surgeon decides whether a drain is needed.
Why it is used
Blood and fluid that collect in the wound after surgery drain out through the tube. If the wound becomes infected and pus forms, it may also drain through the tube.
Types

Most often it is a closed drain with a container: a concertina, a bulb or a bag. Some containers create gentle suction and draw the fluid out softly. A separate treatment is a vacuum dressing. It is sealed over the wound and connected to a device that creates suction. This is not the same as a drain tube.
What is in the container
The container usually holds blood-stained fluid. Over time there is less of it and it becomes lighter. The nurse measures the amount, records it, and empties or changes the container.
Moving with a drain

The drain is secured, and you can move with it. Get up only when staff say so. Keep the container below the wound, do not pull the tube, and make sure it is not kinked or trapped under your body. The container can be attached to your clothes, as the nurse will show you.
What not to do

In hospital, do not open or empty the container yourself. Do not disconnect the tube, squeeze the concertina or touch the dressing unless staff tell you to. If you go home with a drain, the nurse will explain how to look after it at home.
Tell staff straight away

Tell the nurse straight away if the tube has come out, moved or come apart; if the dressing around it is soaked; if a lot of bright red blood is quickly filling the container; if the concertina has expanded; if pain or swelling gets worse, you develop a fever, or the fluid becomes cloudy, pus-like or smells unpleasant.
When it comes out

How long it stays depends on the operation and the amount of fluid. Sometimes the drain is removed after one or two days, sometimes it stays longer. The surgeon decides when to remove it. A nurse or doctor takes it out: it is quick, it may be uncomfortable, and you will be given pain relief if needed. A dressing is put over the tube site.
After removal

In the first hours a little fluid may leak from the drain site; staff will change the dressing. At home, if redness is spreading, pus comes from the wound or the drain site, pain is increasing or you have a fever, get medical help as soon as possible.
